newsitem.title: USA: N.Korea meeting postponed for week to Feb. 5 - U.S..
newsitem.headline: N.Korea meeting postponed for week to Feb. 5 - U.S..

text.p: A briefing for North Korea on proposed Korean peninsula peace talks has been postponed one week to Feb. 5 while Pyongyang tries to complete a grain deal with a U.S. firm to feed its famished people, the State Department said on Monday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters the briefing was moved from Jan. 29 at Pyongyang's request because North Korea wanted to complete grain negotiations with a "private western company," presumably Cargill Inc.

He said the United States and South Korea agreed, and now "we plan to meet next week in New York on February 5 for a briefing on the four-party proposal that was made by (South Korean) President Kim (Young-sam) and President (Bill) Clinton."
Some U.S. officials privately were more skeptical that the meeting -- aimed at briefing North Korea on the proposal for four-party peace talks put forward last year -- would take place then.

North Korea, following months of resistance, agreed in December to attend the crucial U.S.-South Korean briefing after negotiations with Washington that led to Pyongyang apologizing for a September submarine incursion into the South that had fanned new tensions on the Korean peninsula.
Washington and Seoul see the four-party peace talks, which would also include China, as a way to get North and South Korea into direct negotiations on the peninsula's future.

Also as a result of the submarine-related negotiations, Washington approved a license for Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc., the world's largest private grain trading company, to export 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to North Korea in what was expected to be a barter arrangement.

Burns said in seeking postponement of the briefing, "The North Koreans mentioned to us ... that they have put first priority recently on some grain discussions, discussions of the import of grain they're having ... with some private Western companies." Officials said later he referred to Cargill.
He "guessed" North Korea expected to conclude the talks by next week and "that is a satisfactory explanation."

U.S. officials told Reuters North Korea did not make a direct link between successful completion of the Cargill deal and Pyongyang's participation at the peace talks briefing, which was to be on Wednesday.

But they said North Korea may have misunderstood what would be expected of it under such a grain deal or thought Pyongyang could get Washington to front-end some of the costs if the North forced a delay in the peace talks briefing.
Cargill negotiators left North Korea last weekend without a deal but a company spokesman, Lori Johnson, told Reuters "we're continuing to work toward an agreement."
She would not reveal the stumbling blocks but said: "We're not a part of -- in any way, shape or form -- the diplomatic negotiations going on between the various governments."
"In our minds it is a commercial deal and is wholly separate from the diplomatic negotiations that do not include us," she added.
One U.S. official said North Korea apparently thought that after Cargill got the license, Pyongyang would take possession of the grain quickly and then work out payment later.

Burns said he did not know if the United States had been asked to help North Korea finance the deal. "These are private negotiations. So we would rarely step into a negotiation like this. I don't believe we are," he said.

U.S. officials said if the Cargill deal cannot be resolved and Pyongyang again delays the peace talks briefing it would have a negative effect on South Korean public opinion. Seoul has agreed to pay much of the cost of new nuclear reactors for North Korea under a 1994 accord with the United States.

North and South Korea are still technically at war after the 1950-1953 Korean conflict that ended in a truce. North Korea has had serious food shortages recently, and experts say the situation will be dire this year.
